title: 21 Signs You're Poorer Than You Think
description:
A nice car, a decent salary and a new phone can hide a very fragile financial life. In this video I go through 21 signs you might be poorer than you think, from three angles: seven numbers you can check in ten minutes, the psychology that hides the problem, and the weak spots in your safety net, each with a simple fix.

Get The Ryan Rover Money Playbook: [LINK HERE]

Chapters:
0:00 Intro
1:37 How we got the numbers
2:08 Angle 1: The Numbers
2:15 1. You don't know your net worth
3:27 2. You couldn't cover $400 in cash
4:33 3. You save less than 5%
5:41 4. Housing eats more than 30%
6:51 5. Your car loan is six years or longer
7:55 6. You pay only the minimum
9:00 7. Retirement savings are behind
10:11 The ten minute money checkup
11:47 Angle 2: The Psychology
12:06 8. You feel rich on payday
12:59 9. You measure wealth by stuff
13:56 10. You count on future money
14:50 11. You think everyone lives this way
15:58 12. You avoid checking your balance
16:51 13. You use credit to feel normal
17:45 14. You think about money constantly
18:38 Why the brain hides the problem
20:01 Angle 3: The Playbook
20:18 15. One job loss from crisis
21:17 16. One income source
22:12 17. No insurance safety net
23:10 18. No investments outside your home
24:04 19. Paying for convenience you can't afford
24:57 20. Your debt keeps growing
25:52 21. You have no plan
26:45 The couple who looked fine
28:10 Score yourself
29:08 Questions people ask
31:05 Recap: all 21 signs
31:53 What to do next

Sources:
- US Bureau of Economic Analysis, personal saving rate (around 4-5% in recent years)
- Federal Reserve, Survey of Consumer Finances 2022 (median net worth under 35: about $39,040)
- Federal Reserve, Economic Well-Being of U.S. Households in 2024 (63% would cover a $400 expense with cash or its equivalent)
- HUD, cost-burdened households (over 30% of income on housing); Harvard Joint Center for Housing Studies, State of the Nation's Housing
- Edmunds, share of new-car loans of 72 months or longer
- Federal Reserve, G.19 Consumer Credit: credit card interest rates
- Fidelity, retirement savings guideline (1x salary by 30, 3x by 40, 6x by 50, 8x by 60, 10x by 67)
- Social Security Administration (benefits replace about 40% of pre-retirement income for the average worker)
- Thomas J. Stanley, income statement vs balance sheet affluent; Mullainathan and Shafir, Scarcity (2013)
- American Psychological Association, Stress in America surveys; BLS JOLTS layoffs and discharges; Federal Reserve Bank of New York, Household Debt and Credit Report
- Growth example: monthly compounding at 7% average yearly return (illustration, not a promise)

Photos: Wikimedia Commons contributors. Full credits and licenses: https://github.com/ryan-rover-money-channel/ryan-rover-money/blob/main/agendamento/creditos/video23.md

This video is for education only and is not financial advice. Numbers are illustrations, not promises.
